newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Candidates supplant parties in Venezuela elections.
newsitem.headline: Candidates supplant parties in Venezuela elections.

text.p: A former beauty queen leads the polls. A failed coupster has vowed to take power through the ballot box. And a disgraced former president has served notice that his political career is not dead and buried.
With less than 18 months to Venezuela's presidential elections, the political scene has all the makings of one of the country's celebrated soap operas.

But the plethora of candidates, and paucity of ideas, could signal a sea-change in Venezuela's political map as voters turn away from the two traditional parties that have dominated for five decades, analysts and politicians said.
"There's more talk about polls than about ideas," said Senator Eduardo Gomez Tamayo, a member of the ruling Convergence party.
"It's obvious that there has been a change in attitude. People are more demanding about what they expect," the former president of Congress added.
The new mood of public opinion has sent parties scurrying for candidates who can catch a jaded public's imagination.

Social democratic Democratic Action (AD) and social Christian Copei are the dominant forces in Venezuelan politics, but the level of disillusionment has forced even these parties to widen their nets for potential candidates.
"There's a frantic-ness, a sense of casting about," said independent political consultant Erik Ekvall.
Nowhere is the search more intense than in social Christian party Copei, which has not won a presidential election since Luis Herrera Campins' triumph in 1978.
At a recent soul-searching weekend by Copei top brass, the party agreed to allow an outsider to become its candidate.
"Copei's opening up is interesting, though it is an admission of its own weakness," said Claudio Fermin, AD's presidential candidate in 1993 and a front-runner to lead the party in 1998.
Top of Copei's shopping list appears to be former Miss Universe Irene Saez -- who is so far the axis of the elections.

Aged just 35, Saez has become the candidate to beat. Overwhelmingly re-elected mayor of Caracas district Chacao in 1995, Saez tops opinion polls with anywhere from 40 to 50 percent of popular support, while her closest rival gets only around 10 percent.
Saez makes little secret of her desire to take the country's top job, but has been careful not to formally announce her bid and to maintain her edge as an independent.

"People are waiting for a political leader, a messiah...and I'm realizing that people are pointing to me," Saez said in a recent interview. Critics say the statuesque blonde has no concrete policies and limited experience.
A Saez candidacy, either backed by Copei or by a range of other parties, is almost a certainty, if only as an outlet for popular discontent, analysts said.

"If Irene didn't exist, we would have to invent her," political analyst Anibal Romero said in a newspaper interview. "She personifies aspirations which don't have alternative channels. That's why she heads the polls."
The only visible threat to Saez so far may be voter apathy -- which would benefit AD as the only party with a machine capable of really delivering votes.
AD candidates, backed by the most sophisticated party apparatus in the country, swept over half the state governorships in 1995 local elections when turnout was under 40 percent.

The Saez phenomenon is seen by many as a reaction to President Rafael Caldera's government. Though he broke with Copei to lead Convergence to power in 1993, the 81-year-old leader is seen as the creator of the much-maligned political establishment.
Saez' name is not the only one to come out of the political outfield to join the potpourri of potential candidates.

Luis Giusti, who has led an unprecedented opening of the state oil industry as president of Petroleos de Venezuela (PdVSA) has been fingered by both Copei and union-based Radical Cause (Causa R) politicians, reflecting a new mobility in political boundaries.
"You could see some very strange bedfellows," said Ekvall.

Retired Lt. Col. Hugo Chavez, the leader of a failed 1992 coup attempt and Carlos Andres Perez, who survived Chavez's challenge, but was later ousted and jailed on corruption charges, also plan to play a part in the electoral scene, though most analysts see their impact as small.
And with Causa R and Movement to Socialism (MAS) parties both undergoing public internal splits, AD continues to hold most of the cards, particularly if voter disinterest continues, analysts said.
